Day 7 of GRC PULSE.

Search job listings for "GRC Professional" and you'll find almost none. Recent UK hiring data shows the actual titles doing GRC work are scattered — Analyst tops the list at roughly a quarter of roles, then Consultant, then Architect, Security Analyst, and Risk Analyst make up most of the rest.
That's not a data quirk. 

It reflects something true about the role itself: GRC isn't one job. It's a function that shows up inside a lot of different jobs.
So what does a GRC professional actually do, regardless of the title on the org chart?

They translate between languages that don't naturally understand each other. A security team talks in vulnerabilities and technical severity. Executives talk in budget and business impact. Regulators talk in specific legal requirements. A GRC professional is often the person who can hold all three conversations and connect them.
They ask uncomfortable questions early, instead of urgent ones late. Before a new vendor gets access to customer data, before a product launches, before a system goes live — the GRC professional is the one asking "what happens if this goes wrong, and are we allowed to do this."

They build and maintain the paper trail that proves things happened. Not because paperwork is the point, but because when a regulator, auditor, or customer asks "how do you know you're managing this risk," an answer without evidence isn't really an answer.

They don't own the risk. This one matters. A GRC professional identifies risk, assesses it, and helps decide how to treat it — but the actual risk belongs to the business function that created it. A GRC analyst flagging a vulnerability doesn't make the vulnerability their fault; it makes visibility their job.
Picture a mid-sized company rolling out a new AI vendor for HR data. The GRC professional isn't the one configuring the tool or negotiating the contract price. They're the one asking what data the vendor can access, whether that's covered under existing agreements, what happens if the vendor has a breach, and who signs off before this goes live.

The business impact of not having someone doing this work isn't always visible immediately. It shows up later — during an incident nobody assessed in advance, or an audit that surfaces a decision nobody can explain.

Practical takeaway: if your title doesn't say "GRC" but your job involves asking "are we allowed to do this, and can we prove it," you're already doing GRC work. The title catches up eventually. The function usually starts first.

A sudden 2x spike in job postings across major firms usually signals one thing. 
It is rarely just normal attrition. 
It points to a newly funded push, a major transformation project, or teams scaling up after a hiring freeze. 

When you see companies tripling their open roles overnight, the smartest move is not just throwing your resume into the portal. 
It is understanding why those roles exist and where your specific leverage lies. 

Here is how to approach high-growth hiring waves strategically:
1. Look past the volume and decode the operational need. 
A massive surge in enterprise hiring often points to scaling delivery challenges, route-to-market expansions, or large-scale digital transformations. 

2. Position yourself as an efficiency multiplier. 
In complex IT and go-to-market ecosystems, companies are not just looking for headcount. They want professionals who can design AI-powered automations, slash manual triage, and optimize workflows using LLMs and low-code tools. 

3. Speak the language of measurable impact. 
Whether you are managing global software programs, cutting support triage times by 60%, or negotiating multi-million dollar contracts, hiring managers want to see the bottom-line metrics behind your delivery. 

4. Leverage cross-functional alignment. 
Rapid scaling breaks silos. Highlight your experience in bridging pricing operations, IT, and external vendors to hit fixed delivery dates without friction. 

When the market accelerates, generic applications get lost in the noise. 

Targeted, value-driven positioning cuts straight through it.

A 9-year lease. A workforce plan nobody can defend past 18 months.

That is the position most enterprise occupiers in India are sitting in right now.

The lease structure has not changed. 3+3+3. Lock-in of three to five years. Escalation every three. Six months notice. Deposit blocked. A restoration obligation at the end that most finance teams have not provisioned for.

What changed is the input.

Ask a CHRO today what headcount looks like in 2029 and the honest answer is that they do not know. Support and L1 functions are being rebuilt around AI. Some teams are contracting. Data, platform and applied AI teams are hiring faster than the fit-out was ever designed for. The total number may land flat. The shape will not.

So the commitment runs nine years and the confidence runs six quarters.

That gap gets paid for one of two ways. Empty desks still carrying rent, CAM, power and amortised capex. Or a scramble for space at short notice at whatever the market is charging that quarter.

The fix is not a shorter lease. Landlords are not offering them on good product, and they should not.

The fix is structural. Hold the core on lease. Put the volatility in managed space.

The part of the business you cannot forecast belongs in a contract you can adjust.

Most occupiers are still treating a forecasting problem as a real estate problem.

If your lease outlives your workforce plan by seven years, that is worth an hour with finance and HR this quarter.

A few people have asked me about the AI Essentials credential this week, and what actually makes it different from the hundreds of AI courses sitting on LinkedIn right now. Fair question. I'd rather answer it properly than sell around it.

Anyone can print a certificate. I've collected plenty of them over the years. Sat through the day, taken the photo, gone home with a PDF. They're in a drawer or a filing cabinet somewhere and nobody has ever asked to see one.

A credential has to do four things, and most training does none of them.

It needs a published body of knowledge, so you can see exactly what is being tested before you commit anyone's time or budget to it. It needs governance that sits outside the people selling the training, because a provider that marks its own homework is really just writing itself a brochure. It needs an assessment you can genuinely fail. And it needs to be verifiable by somebody who wasn't in the room, whether that's a hiring manager, a client, a procurement team or an auditor. If the only proof is an image the candidate emails you himself, then you're trusting the candidate, not the standard.

The sharpest test I know is whether the thing can be taken away.

A certificate records that you turned up on a Tuesday, and nobody can retract a Tuesday. A credential is a live claim about what somebody can do, and a live claim can be withdrawn if the ability isn't there any more. That's uncomfortable. It's also exactly why it carries weight.

It matters more now than it did two years ago, because the competence of your people is starting to show up inside contracts and tender documents. A filing cabinet full of Tuesdays won't answer those.

So hold your next training provider against all four before you sign anything. Even if it isn't us.

And tell me what you'd add. I've been building this list from what I keep running into across Thailand and Malaysia, so I'd rather have it picked apart than agreed with.

💼 Why Are IT Companies Laying Off Employees While Still Hiring in 2026?

The IT industry is not simply “shrinking.”

It is restructuring.

In India, hiring is becoming more selective, especially in traditional IT services. Recent reports show hiring momentum weakening in IT-BPM, while demand is shifting toward AI, cloud, cybersecurity, data engineering, platform engineering, and other specialised roles.

At the same time, AI is changing the economics of software delivery.

Clients increasingly expect:

⚡ Faster execution
📉 Lower delivery cost
📈 Higher productivity
🎯 Outcome-based contracts
🤖 AI-enabled teams

This is forcing IT services companies to rethink the old model of adding more people for every new project. Reuters reports that India’s IT services sector is moving away from traditional headcount-heavy billing toward productivity- and outcome-based contracts, while automation reduces the need for some routine coding work.

So why are layoffs happening?

1. Routine work is being automated
Basic coding, repetitive testing, support tasks, documentation, and some operational work can now be completed faster with AI-assisted tools.

2. Clients are demanding more with smaller teams A team of 10 AI-enabled engineers may now be expected to deliver what previously required a much larger delivery team.

3. Companies are correcting their workforce pyramid
Some firms are reducing middle layers while rebuilding teams around fewer managers, AI-enabled engineers, and specialised technical talent.

The strongest demand is increasingly around:

🧠 AI / GenAI
☁️ Cloud
🔐 Cybersecurity
📊 Data Engineering
⚙️ Platform Engineering
🏗️ Architecture
🤖 AI-integrated Full-Stack Development

5. The location of hiring is also changing
Global Capability Centres are becoming an increasingly important source of technology employment in India and have been adding talent faster than traditional IT services firms.

This creates an interesting contradiction:

Layoffs can rise while demand for strong engineers also rises.

The market is not saying:

❌ “We don't need developers.”

It is increasingly saying:

✅ “We need fewer people doing repetitive execution and more people who can solve complex problems.”

That changes what companies value.

A developer who only knows how to execute a predefined task is under more pressure.

A developer who can understand:

Business Requirement → Architecture → UI/UX → API → Data → Security → Cloud → AI → Deployment

becomes significantly more valuable.

💡 My observation as an IT agency owner:

The next phase of the IT industry will not be about building the largest teams.

It will be about building smaller, highly capable, AI-enabled teams that can take greater ownership of the complete product..

55% of California firms plan to grow headcount this year 📈

And nearly 4 in 5 say hiring qualified professionals is at least moderately difficult

When asked how they plan to close the talent gap, firms reached for automation first (49%), ahead of flexible work, contract staff, and higher pay.

But while adoption is fairly widespread, it's not yet ingrained into processes. 

56% use generative AI somewhere in the firm, but only 10% have it integrated across most operations. The leading use cases are email drafting, document review and tax research. Genuinely useful, but not life changing.

Meanwhile the back office is still largely manual at roughly 4 in 10 firms for receipt collection, month-end close and AP. Only 18% say their systems work together seamlessly.

What I take from it on the hiring side - 63% describe their firm's core value today as compliance and technical work. Five years out, 64% expect to be seen primarily as advisers. That is close to a full reversal, and technology fluency now ranks as the number one skill firms expect to matter over the next decade.

The "AI is going to take our jobs" gets clicks, but it isn't the full story. Automation won't take your job if you adapt and up-skill in areas that AI and automation cannot do. My one piece of advice to candidates who are worried about AI is "become irreplaceable."

Unless you plan to retire in the next couple of years, this is something that anyone working in the tax profession should be thinking about and getting ahead of - the pace of tech/AI advancement is only getting quicker.

What are your thoughts? Do you think CPAs should be more worried?

**Stop building brittle open-source AI agent stacks for smart home and real estate tech that leave no audit trail, no replay, and no durable state.**

I learned this the hard way after a tenant-screening bot dropped its reasoning chain mid-conversation and we rebuilt the decision log by hand. That failure pushed us toward open-source agent stacks that actually behave like production software.

1. Use the Cowork pattern to turn every agent step into a durable, replayable event instead of a fragile chain of API calls.

2. Start with Spec Kit to write the contract before the code: inputs, outputs, and invariants for a real estate task like lease abstraction or energy scheduling.

3. Adopt JustHireMe-style routing to assign the right specialized agent to the right job, rather than asking one oversized model to be a leasing expert, a maintenance triage nurse, and a compliance auditor.

4. Keep durable state so a smart home automation or property-management bot survives restarts, retries, and multi-day approval workflows without starting from zero.

5. Run a local LLM on Apple Silicon when tenant data, floor plans, or access logs should stay on-device. Ollama or MLX get qwen2.5-coder running on M1–M4 hardware without sending prompts to the cloud.

6. Vibe code the boilerplate first, then use Spec Kit to lock the contract and Cowork to make execution traceable. The speed helps you ship, but the rigor keeps agents from hallucinating in production.

This workflow changed how I think about reliability: agentic systems only graduate from demo to product when you can replay the exact path that produced a decision. If you are hiring or leveling up, this skill set separates toy demos from deployable PropTech systems.

What is the most painful agent failure you have had to debug, and would a replayable trace have saved you?

What Should Founders Know About Human In The Loop?

It seems now that every founder is being told to use AI. Automate customer service. Automate marketing. Automate sales. Automate bookkeeping. Automate hiring. Automate everything.

But we know there is a problem with that advice.

AI is incredibly good at producing answers. It's not nearly as good at knowing when the answer matters enough to require a human.

That is where “Human In The Loop” becomes important.

Human In The Loop, or HITL, simply means designing an AI-enabled process where a person remains involved at critical points. The machine does the heavy lifting. The human reviews, challenges, approves, corrects or intervenes.

For founders, this matters.

The objective of AI should not be to eliminate humans from your business. It should be to eliminate the work humans should not be doing.

Let AI summarize 500 customer comments. Let a human decide what product change they imply.

Let AI prepare the first draft of a contract. Let a lawyer decide whether you should sign it.

Let AI identify unusual financial transactions. Let someone who understands the business determine whether they actually make sense.

Let AI screen information. Be very careful about letting it make irreversible decisions.

The more consequential the decision, the more important the human becomes. This is especially true because AI can make a dangerous kind of mistake: A very convincing one.

An inexperienced employee who doesn't know something may hesitate. But AI is rarely nervous. It can produce a polished, articulate and completely incorrect answer with remarkable confidence. 

That creates a new management challenge. Your employees need to learn not merely how to use AI, but importantly, when not to trust it.

And that may become one of the most valuable skills inside a company. 

Founders should therefore stop asking: “How much of this process can we automate?” And start asking: “Where does human judgment create the most value?”

Those are very different questions.

The best AI-enabled companies may not be the companies with the fewest humans. They may be the companies that become exceptionally good at deciding where humans belong.

Automate repetition, retrieval, first drafts, and pattern recognition.

But keep humans close to ambiguity, judgment, ethics, relationships, exceptions and decisions where being wrong is expensive.

The future isn't Human or Machine. It's Human with Machine.

And founders who understand how to design that relationship will have an enormous advantage over founders who simply automate everything they can.

A question I've learned to ask our firm's clients: "If your AI made a serious mistake tomorrow, where in your business would a human catch it before your customer does?"

Do you know?

Most companies measure AI agents by how many people they replace. The better metric: how many days they remove from a decision.

When an executive evaluates an AI project, the first question is usually cost savings. Headcount reduction is easy to model, but it is the wrong lens.

AI agents should be treated as decision-speed infrastructure.

A pricing change that used to take days of analysis can be re-run in hours. A lead qualification decision that depended on a weekly meeting can happen the moment new data arrives. A contract review that held up a deal can be compressed into minutes.

This is not about making a slow process slightly faster. It is about compounding advantage.

Every cycle that gets shorter in pricing, sales, hiring, or operations creates follow-on effects across the business. The company that decides faster learns faster. The company that learns faster improves faster.

Decision latency is a better measure of AI value than labor savings because it captures strategic upside rather than cost avoidance.

That does not make headcount irrelevant. It just means cost savings are the floor, not the ceiling.

The real question is not “how much will we save by deploying AI agents?” It is “how much faster can we make the decisions that matter?”

If you are evaluating AI agents, start by mapping your slowest, highest-value decisions. Find where weeks turn into days and days turn into hours. A strategy consultation can help you identify the decisions worth compressing.
